algorithms: QuickSort always picks the first element as the pivot. What is its running time on an array that is already sorted?
Each partition splits off only the pivot, so the recursion depth is n and the total work is n + (n-1) + ... + 1, which is O(n^2).
How much auxiliary memory does a standard top-down MergeSort on an array of n elements use?
Merging two sorted halves needs a temporary buffer proportional to n. Only the recursion stack is O(log n), the buffer dominates.
You must sort records by date while keeping records with the same date in their original order. Which algorithm guarantees this?
MergeSort is stable when ties are taken from the left half first. Heapsort, typical in-place QuickSort and array selection sort can reorder equal keys.
What is the lower bound on the worst-case number of comparisons for any comparison-based sorting algorithm on n elements?
A decision tree that distinguishes all n! orderings has height at least log2(n!), which is Omega(n log n). Non-comparison sorts like counting sort avoid this bound.
Roughly how many comparisons does binary search need in the worst case to find a value in a sorted array of 1,000,000 elements?
Each step halves the range, so it needs about log2(1,000,000), which is close to 20 steps.
Binary search uses lo = 0, hi = n, while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2. When a[mid] < target, which update is correct and avoids an infinite loop?
a[mid] is too small, so the answer lies strictly right of mid. Setting lo = mid can loop forever when hi = lo + 1.
Which condition must hold for binary search on an array to return correct results?
The array is sorted by the search key
The array has no duplicate values
The array length is a power of two
The array is stored in a linked list
Binary search discards half the range based on order, which only works if the elements are sorted. Duplicates and odd lengths are fine.
Which algorithm finds the path with the fewest edges from a source vertex in an unweighted graph?
BFS visits vertices in order of distance in edges, so the first time it reaches a vertex is along a shortest path. DFS may reach it through a long path first.
An iterative depth-first search replaces the recursion with which data structure?
DFS goes deep first, which is last-in first-out order, so it uses a stack. A queue gives BFS order instead.
What is the time complexity of BFS or DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges stored as adjacency lists?
Each vertex is visited once and each adjacency list is scanned once. O(V^2) applies to an adjacency matrix.
During DFS on a directed graph, you reach a neighbor that is still on the current recursion stack. What does this show?
An edge to an ancestor still on the stack is a back edge, and a back edge in a directed graph means a cycle exists.
Which property of a graph can make Dijkstra's algorithm return wrong shortest distances?
Dijkstra assumes a vertex's distance is final once it is extracted, which breaks when a later negative edge could shorten it. Zero weights are fine.
After V - 1 rounds of Bellman-Ford, one extra round still relaxes some edge. What does this indicate?
A negative cycle is reachable from the source
Some vertex cannot be reached from the source at all
The source has no outgoing edges in the graph
All edge weights in the graph are positive
Without negative cycles, shortest paths have at most V - 1 edges and are final after V - 1 rounds. Any further improvement proves a negative cycle.
What is the time complexity of the Bellman-Ford algorithm on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
It relaxes all E edges in each of V - 1 rounds. O(E log V) is Dijkstra with a binary heap, and O(V^3) is Floyd-Warshall.
What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm using a binary heap on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
Each vertex is extracted once and each edge may cause a decrease-key or push, and every heap operation costs O(log V).
Which two properties make a problem a good fit for dynamic programming?
Sorted input and a greedy choice property
Constant input size and random access
DP pays off when the same subproblems repeat and an optimal answer is built from optimal sub-answers. Disjoint subproblems suit plain divide and conquer.
The naive recursive fib(n) takes exponential time. What is the time complexity after adding memoization?
Each value fib(0) to fib(n) is computed once and then reused, and each computation does O(1) work.
What is the time complexity of the standard DP for 0/1 knapsack with n items and integer capacity W?
The table has n * W cells, each filled in O(1). This is pseudo-polynomial, since W can be exponential in its number of bits.
For activity selection (choose the most non-overlapping intervals), which greedy rule is provably optimal?
Pick the interval that finishes earliest
Pick the interval that starts earliest
Pick the interval with the fewest overlaps
Choosing the earliest finish leaves the most room for the rest, and an exchange argument proves it optimal. The other rules have counterexamples.
With coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6, compare greedy (always take the largest coin that fits) with the optimal solution.
Both use 2 coins, so greedy is optimal
Both use 3 coins, so greedy is optimal
Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins), while 3 + 3 needs only 2. Greedy change-making is only optimal for certain coin systems.
data-structures: In a dynamic array (like a Python list or C++ vector) that doubles its capacity when full, what is the amortized cost of appending one element?
O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
Occasional O(n) copies are spread over many cheap appends; total copy work stays below 2n, so each append is O(1) amortized.
What is the cost of accessing the k-th element of a singly linked list that has only a head pointer?
O(k)
O(log k)
A linked list has no random access, so you follow k next pointers from the head.
Which technique detects whether a singly linked list has a cycle using O(1) extra memory?
Slow and fast pointers (Floyd's algorithm)
Sorting the nodes by their memory address
Storing visited nodes in a hash set
Reversing the list twice and comparing heads
A fast pointer moving two steps meets a slow pointer moving one step only if there is a cycle. A hash set also works but uses O(n) memory.
In a doubly linked list, you have a pointer to a node in the middle. What is the cost of removing that node?
O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
The node knows both neighbors, so you relink prev.next and next.prev directly without traversing the list.
Starting with an empty stack: push 1, push 2, push 3, pop, push 4, pop, pop. Which element remains on the stack?
Pops remove 3, then 4, then 2 (last in, first out), leaving only 1.
Which data structure is the standard choice for checking whether brackets in a string like ([]{}) are balanced?
A stack
A queue
A min-heap
A trie
Each closing bracket must match the most recent unmatched opening bracket, which is exactly last-in first-out order.
Starting with an empty queue: enqueue 1, enqueue 2, enqueue 3, dequeue, enqueue 4, dequeue. What is now at the front?
Dequeues remove 1 and then 2 (first in, first out), so 3 is at the front, followed by 4.
A queue is implemented with two stacks (an inbox and an outbox). What is the amortized cost per enqueue or dequeue?
O(log n)
O(n)
O(sqrt n)
Each element is pushed and popped at most twice in total, so even though one transfer can be O(n), the amortized cost is O(1).
A hash table uses chaining and a bad hash function sends all n keys to the same bucket. What is the lookup time?
O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
All keys sit in one chain, so a lookup scans a list of length n. The O(1) average assumes keys spread evenly.
Why does a hash table grow and rehash when its load factor (items per bucket) gets too high?
To keep chains short and operations O(1) on average
To keep the keys in sorted order for range scans
To remove duplicate keys that pile up in the same bucket
To reduce the total memory the table uses
A high load factor means more collisions and longer probe sequences. Resizing restores a low load factor, at the cost of more memory.
What happens when you run d = {}; d[[1, 2]] = 3 in Python?
It raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
It stores the key as the tuple (1, 2)
It stores the value under the key 1
It silently creates an empty dict
Dict keys must be hashable, and lists are mutable and unhashable. Use a tuple (1, 2) as the key instead.
Which traversal of a binary search tree visits the keys in ascending sorted order?
In-order
Pre-order
Post-order
Level-order
In-order visits left subtree, then node, then right subtree, which matches the BST ordering property.
You insert the keys 1, 2, 3, ..., n in order into a plain (unbalanced) BST. What is the worst-case search time afterwards?
O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
Every new key becomes a right child, so the tree degenerates into a linked list of height n. Self-balancing trees prevent this.
What invariant does an AVL tree maintain at every node?
Subtree heights differ by at most 1
Both subtrees have equal size
Every node has exactly two children
Left child keys equal the parent key
The AVL balance factor is kept in {-1, 0, 1} by rotations, which keeps the height O(log n).
Which of these is one of the rules of a red-black tree?
A red node cannot have a red child
Every leaf (NIL) node must be red
The root node must be colored red
Every path has the same number of red nodes
Red-black trees forbid two reds in a row and require the same number of black nodes on every root-to-leaf path, which bounds the height at O(log n).
A binary heap is stored in a 0-indexed array. What is the index of the parent of the element at index i (for i > 0)?
With 0-based indexing, children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, so the parent of i is (i - 1) // 2. 2i + 1 is the left child.
What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from n unsorted elements with bottom-up heapify (sift-down from the last parent)?
O(n)
O(n log n)
O(log n)
Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a short distance; summing the heights gives O(n). Inserting one by one is O(n log n).
You need the k largest values from a stream of n numbers using little memory. Which approach is the standard choice?
Keep a min-heap of size k, O(n log k)
Keep a max-heap of all n values, O(n)
Sort the stream at the end, O(n)
Keep a stack of size k, O(n)
The min-heap root is the smallest of the current top k, so each new value is compared with it and swapped in if larger, using O(k) memory.
A road graph has 1,000,000 vertices and 3,000,000 edges. Which representation is usually the right choice?
Adjacency list
Adjacency matrix
Incidence matrix
Edge list sorted by weight
The graph is sparse. An adjacency matrix would need 10^12 cells, while adjacency lists use O(V + E) memory.
What is the time to check whether a word of length L exists in a trie that holds N words?
O(L)
O(log N)
O(N)
O(L * N)
A trie lookup follows one edge per character, independent of how many words are stored. That is why tries suit prefix search and autocomplete.
competitive-programming: A problem has n up to 2 * 10^5 and a time limit of 1 second. Which time complexity is a safe target?
O(n log n)
O(n^2 log n)
n log n is about 3.6 million operations, well within a second. n^2 is 4 * 10^10, far above the roughly 10^8 simple operations per second rule of thumb.
What is the time complexity of this loop: i = 1; while i < n: i = i * 2?
O(log n)
O(n)
O(sqrt n)
O(n log n)
i doubles each iteration, so it reaches n after about log2(n) steps.
You have a sorted array and pointers at both ends to find a pair with sum equal to target. The current sum is less than target. What should you do?
Move the left pointer one step right
Move the right pointer one step left
Move both pointers inward
Restart from the middle
Moving the left pointer right increases the sum, because the array is sorted. Moving the right pointer left would make it smaller.
What is the time complexity of the standard 3Sum solution (sort, then two pointers for each fixed first element)?
O(n log n)
O(n)
Sorting is O(n log n), then for each of n elements the two-pointer scan is O(n), giving O(n^2) overall.
You need the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of fixed length k. With a sliding window, how do you update the sum when the window moves one step?
Add the new element and subtract the leaving one
Recompute the sum of all k elements from scratch
Multiply the sum by the ratio of new to old element
Add the new element only, keeping the old ones
Each shift changes only two elements, so updating in O(1) gives O(n) total instead of O(n * k).
What is the length of the longest substring without repeating characters in abcabcbb?
abc is the longest window with all distinct characters. A sliding window with a last-seen map finds it in O(n).
Which data structure gives O(n) total time for computing the maximum of every window of size k in an array?
A monotonic deque
A binary search tree
A hash map
A segment tree
A deque keeps candidate indices in decreasing value order, and each index is pushed and popped once. A segment tree or BST would give O(n log k) or O(n log n).
For a positive integer x, what does x & (x - 1) compute?
x with its lowest set bit cleared
x with its highest set bit cleared
Only the lowest set bit of x
The number of set bits in x
Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and the zeros below it, so ANDing clears exactly that bit. For example, 12 & 11 is 8.
Which expression correctly tests whether an integer x is a power of two?
A power of two has exactly one set bit, so clearing the lowest set bit gives zero. x > 0 excludes zero. (x & 1) == 0 only tests evenness.
What is the value of 5 ^ 3 in C++, Java or Python, where ^ is bitwise XOR?
101 XOR 011 is 110, which is 6. In these languages ^ is XOR, not exponentiation.
Every number in an array appears exactly twice except one, which appears once. What finds that number in O(n) time and O(1) space?
XOR all the elements together
Add all elements and divide by 2
AND all the elements together
Sort and take the middle element
a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a, so the paired values cancel and only the single value remains.
For x = 12 (binary 1100) in two's complement, what is x & -x?
x & -x isolates the lowest set bit. In 1100 that bit is worth 4. Fenwick trees rely on this trick.
A segment tree over n elements supports point update and range sum query. What is the cost of each operation?
O(log n)
O(sqrt n)
O(n)
Both walk a path from root to leaf and touch O(log n) nodes. Building the tree takes O(n).
For a recursive segment tree over n elements stored in an array, how large is the array usually allocated to be safe for any n?
4n
n
2n
n log n
When n is not a power of two, the tree can use indices beyond 2n, and 4n is a proven safe bound.
What does lazy propagation add to a segment tree?
Range updates in O(log n)
Point queries in O(1)
Building the tree in O(1)
Sorting the array in O(n)
Pending updates are stored at internal nodes and pushed down only when needed, so updating a whole range costs O(log n) instead of O(n).
With both path compression and union by rank, what is the amortized cost per union-find operation?
O(alpha(n)) amortized
O(log n) amortized
O(sqrt n) amortized
O(1) in the worst case
Tarjan proved the inverse Ackermann bound, which is at most 4 or 5 for any practical n, but it is amortized, not worst case per operation.
While adding edges of an undirected graph to a union-find structure, find(u) == find(v) for a new edge (u, v). What does this mean?
Adding the edge would create a cycle
The graph is now fully connected
u and v have no common neighbor
The edge is a bridge of the graph
u and v are already in the same component, so a new edge closes a cycle. Kruskal's algorithm skips such edges.
The modulus p = 10^9 + 7 is prime. How do you compute the modular inverse of a (with a not divisible by p)?
pow(a, p - 2, p)
pow(a, p - 1, p)
pow(a, p, p)
(p - a) % p
By Fermat's little theorem a^(p-1) is 1 mod p, so a^(p-2) is the inverse. a^(p-1) is always 1.
In C++, (a - b) % m can be negative when a < b. Which expression always gives a result in [0, m)?
abs(a - b) % m
C++ % keeps the sign of the dividend, so adding m and taking % m again shifts the result into range. abs gives a different value, and the other forms stay negative or reach m or more.
What does pow(3, 4, 5) return in Python?
3^4 is 81, and 81 mod 5 is 1. The three-argument pow computes modular exponentiation efficiently.
unit-testing: What is the order of the steps in the classic test-driven development cycle?
Red, Green, Refactor
Green, Red, Refactor
Refactor, Red, Green
Red, Refactor, Green
First write a failing test (red), then the simplest code that passes (green), then clean up the code with the tests as a safety net (refactor).
In the Green step of TDD, how much production code should you write?
Just enough to make the failing test pass
The complete feature with all edge cases
Enough to pass the next three planned tests
Nothing until the code is refactored
TDD grows the code in small steps driven by tests. Extra code written ahead of tests is untested and is added only when a new failing test asks for it.
In Python unittest, self.assertEqual(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) fails. Which assertion fixes the test?
self.assertAlmostEqual(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)
self.assertIs(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)
self.assertTrue(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
self.assertIn(0.3, [0.1 + 0.2])
0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in binary floating point. assertAlmostEqual compares after rounding to 7 decimal places by default.
In pytest, how do you assert that calling parse('') raises ValueError?
with pytest.raises(ValueError): parse('')
assert parse('') == ValueError
assert raises(parse(''), ValueError)
pytest.expect(ValueError, parse(''))
pytest.raises is a context manager that fails the test if the block does not raise the given exception. The other forms call parse first, so the exception escapes.
In Jest, expect({ a: 1 }).toBe({ a: 1 }) fails. Which matcher compares the objects by value?
toEqual
toBeTruthy
toBeDefined
toHaveLength
toBe uses Object.is, which checks reference identity, and two object literals are different references. toEqual compares recursively by value.
Which test double mainly returns canned answers to calls and does not verify how it was called?
Stub
Mock
Spy
Dummy
A stub supplies preset return values. A mock is set up with expectations about calls, a spy records calls, and a dummy is passed but never used.
In Jest, you call jest.spyOn(obj, 'save') without any mock implementation. What happens when the code calls obj.save()?
The original method runs and the call is recorded
The call returns undefined and is recorded
The call throws until a return value is set
The original method runs and nothing is recorded
By default jest.spyOn wraps the real method, so it still executes while the spy tracks calls. Use mockImplementation or mockReturnValue to replace it.
Tests replace a real PostgreSQL repository with a working in-memory implementation that stores data in a dictionary. Which kind of test double is this?
Fake
Stub
Dummy
Spy
A fake has real working behavior with a shortcut, such as an in-memory store. A stub only returns fixed values.
Module app.py does from requests import get and calls get(url). In tests of app, which target should unittest.mock.patch replace?
'app.get'
'requests.get'
'requests.api.get'
'builtins.get'
Patch where the name is looked up. app already holds its own reference to get, so patching requests.get leaves app.get unchanged.
With Python unittest.mock, how do you check that mock_send was called exactly once with the argument 5?
mock_send.assert_called_once_with(5)
assert mock_send(5) == 1
mock_send.called_with(5, times=1)
assert mock_send.call_count(5) == 1
assert_called_once_with fails unless there was exactly one call with those arguments. call_count is an attribute, not a function.
A function contains if x > 0: y = 1 with no else branch. One test calls it with x = 5. What coverage does this give for that if statement?
100% line coverage but 50% branch coverage
100% line and 100% branch coverage
50% line coverage and 50% branch coverage
50% line coverage but 100% branch coverage
Every line runs, but the False branch where the condition fails is never taken. Branch coverage is stricter than line coverage.
What does 100% line coverage of a module actually guarantee?
Every line ran at least once
The module contains no bugs
Every branch outcome was tested
Every possible input was checked
Coverage measures execution, not correctness: every line ran at least once during the tests. A line can run with assertions that check nothing, and branches or input ranges can still be untested.
What does mutation testing measure?
Whether tests fail when small bugs are injected
How many lines of code the tests execute
How long the whole test suite takes to run
Whether tests still pass when run in random order
Tools change operators or constants to create mutants. If no test fails, the mutant survives, which shows weak assertions even with high coverage.
A function average(nums) returns sum(nums) / len(nums). Which input is the most important edge case to test?
An empty list, nums = []
A list of one million numbers
A list of positive integers
A list sorted in ascending order
len([]) is 0, so the function raises ZeroDivisionError. The behavior for empty input must be defined and tested.
A field accepts integers from 1 to 100 inclusive. Using boundary value analysis, which set of inputs should you test?
Bugs cluster at boundaries, such as < instead of <=. Testing just inside and just outside each limit catches off-by-one errors.
What is equivalence partitioning in test design?
Testing one value from each class of inputs that behave alike
Running the same test on several machines in parallel at once
Giving every test an equal share of the time budget
Comparing two implementations on randomly generated inputs
If the code treats all values in a class the same way, one representative per class covers it, which cuts redundant tests.
A test fails only around midnight because the code reads the system clock directly. What is the best fix?
Inject a clock the test can control
Retry the test automatically on failure
Skip the test between 23:00 and 01:00
Increase the test timeout
Making time a dependency lets tests set a fixed time, so the result is deterministic. Retries and skips only hide the flakiness.
What distinguishes an integration test from a unit test?
It checks that several real components work together
It always runs in a production environment with real users
It must be written before the code exists
It replaces every dependency with a mock
Integration tests exercise real collaborators, such as a repository with a real database. Unit tests isolate one unit, often with test doubles.
According to the test pyramid, how should a test suite usually be balanced?
Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, fewest end-to-end tests
Many end-to-end tests, fewer integration tests, fewest unit tests
Equal numbers of unit, integration and end-to-end tests
Only end-to-end tests, since they test real user flows
Unit tests are fast and precise, while higher-level tests are slower and more brittle, so the pyramid keeps most tests at the bottom.
Integration tests share one database and pass or fail depending on the order they run in. What is the best fix?
Isolate each test's data, such as rolling back a transaction after it
Run the whole suite twice in a row and keep whichever run had better results
Remove the assertions that depend on data stored in the database
Always run the tests in alphabetical order so results repeat
Order dependence means tests leak state into each other. Giving each test a clean, isolated state makes results independent of order.
linear-algebra: A is a 2x3 matrix and B is a 3x4 matrix. What is the shape of AB?
The inner dimensions (3 and 3) must match and disappear, leaving rows of A by columns of B.
What is the determinant of the 2x2 matrix [[1, 2], [3, 4]]?
For [[a, b], [c, d]] the determinant is ad - bc, which is 1*4 - 2*3 = -2.
Square matrices A and B satisfy det(A) = 2 and det(B) = 3. What is det(AB)?
The determinant is multiplicative: det(AB) = det(A) det(B).
A is a 3x3 matrix with det(A) = 5. What is det(2A)?
Scaling an n x n matrix by c scales the determinant by c^n, so det(2A) = 2^3 * 5 = 40.
What is the dot product of [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6]?
1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6 = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32. The elementwise product [4, 10, 18] is not the dot product.
Two nonzero vectors have a dot product of 0. What does this tell you?
They are orthogonal
They are parallel
They have equal length
One is twice the other
u . v = |u| |v| cos(theta), and with nonzero lengths this is 0 only when cos(theta) = 0, so the angle is 90 degrees.
What is the cosine similarity between [1, 0] and [1, 1]?
About 0.707
Exactly 1.0
Exactly 0.5
About 0.866
The dot product is 1 and the norms are 1 and sqrt(2), so the cosine is 1 / sqrt(2), about 0.707 (an angle of 45 degrees).
What are the eigenvalues of the diagonal matrix [[2, 0], [0, 3]]?
2 and 3
0 and 5
5 and 6
1 and 6
The eigenvalues of a diagonal (or triangular) matrix are its diagonal entries.
What are the eigenvalues of the matrix [[2, 1], [1, 2]]?
1 and 3
2 and 2
0 and 4
-1 and 3
det([[2 - t, 1], [1, 2 - t]]) = (2 - t)^2 - 1 = 0 gives t = 1 or t = 3, with eigenvectors [1, -1] and [1, 1].
A 2x2 matrix has trace 5 and determinant 6. What are its eigenvalues?
2 and 3
1 and 6
1 and 5
-2 and -3
The eigenvalues sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant, and 2 + 3 = 5 with 2 * 3 = 6.
Which property holds for every real symmetric matrix?
Real eigenvalues and an orthogonal set of eigenvectors
Positive eigenvalues and an orthogonal set of eigenvectors
A determinant of 1 and real eigenvalues
Invertible, with all eigenvalues nonzero
The spectral theorem guarantees real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis. Eigenvalues can still be zero or negative, so the other claims fail.
What is the rank of the matrix [[1, 2], [2, 4]]?
The second row is twice the first, so only one row is linearly independent.
Are the vectors (1, 0), (0, 1) and (1, 1) linearly independent in R^2?
No, because three vectors in R^2 must be dependent
Yes, because no two of them are parallel to each other
Yes, because each one has a nonzero entry
No, because (1, 1) is not a unit vector
R^2 has dimension 2, so any 3 vectors are dependent. Indeed (1, 1) = (1, 0) + (0, 1).
A 3x5 matrix has rank 3. What is the dimension of its null space?
By rank-nullity, rank + nullity equals the number of columns, so nullity = 5 - 3 = 2.
Which of these subsets of R^2 is a vector subspace?
The line y = 2x
The line y = 2x + 1
The quadrant x, y >= 0
The circle x^2 + y^2 = 1
A subspace must contain zero and be closed under addition and scaling. y = 2x + 1 misses the origin and the quadrant fails under multiplication by -1.
In the singular value decomposition A = U S V^T, what are the diagonal entries of S?
Nonnegative singular values
The eigenvalues of A, possibly negative
The diagonal entries of A
The Euclidean norms of A's columns
Singular values are square roots of the eigenvalues of A^T A, so they are never negative, and they are usually listed in descending order.
In PCA, the principal directions are the eigenvectors of which matrix?
The covariance matrix of the centered data
The raw data matrix before centering
The identity matrix of the same size
The matrix of pairwise distances between rows
PCA finds directions of maximum variance, which are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ordered by eigenvalue.
Which preprocessing step is required before computing PCA on a data matrix?
Subtract the mean of each feature
Sort the rows by the first feature
Square every value in the matrix
Remove every negative value
Without centering, the first component points toward the mean instead of the direction of greatest variance. Scaling features is also common when units differ.
According to the Eckart-Young theorem, how do you get the best rank-k approximation of a matrix (in Frobenius norm)?
Keep the k largest singular values in the SVD
Keep the first k rows of the matrix
Keep the k largest entries of the matrix
Keep the k smallest singular values in the SVD
Truncated SVD minimizes the approximation error among all rank-k matrices. The error equals the root of the sum of squares of the dropped singular values.
A PCA on centered data gives covariance eigenvalues 5, 3 and 2. What fraction of the total variance does the first component explain?
The total variance is 5 + 3 + 2 = 10, and the first component accounts for 5 / 10 = 50%.
statistics: Salaries in a team are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 100 (thousand dollars). Which measure best describes a typical salary?
The median, 3
The mean, 22
The mode, 100
The range, 99
The single outlier pulls the mean up to 22, while the median is unaffected. The median is robust to outliers.
What is the median of 7, 1, 3, 9?
Sorted, the values are 1, 3, 7, 9. With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values, (3 + 7) / 2 = 5.
What is the mode of 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4?
The mode is the most frequent value, and 3 appears three times.
Household incomes form a strongly right-skewed distribution. How do the mean and median usually compare?
The mean is greater than the median
The mean is less than the median
The mean equals the median
The median is undefined
A long right tail of very high incomes pulls the mean up, while the median stays near the center of the bulk.
What is the population standard deviation of 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9?
The mean is 5, the squared deviations sum to 32, the population variance is 32 / 8 = 4, and the square root is 2.
Why does the sample variance divide by n - 1 instead of n?
So it is an unbiased estimate of the population variance
So it is always smaller than the true population variance
So that it equals the sample standard deviation
So the formula still works when n = 1
Deviations are measured from the sample mean, which makes them slightly too small. Dividing by n - 1 (Bessel's correction) removes that bias.
You add 10 to every value in a dataset. What happens to the standard deviation?
It stays the same
It increases by 10
It is multiplied by 10
It increases by 100
Shifting all values moves the mean by the same amount, so every deviation from the mean is unchanged.
You multiply every value in a dataset by 3. What happens to the variance?
It is multiplied by 9
It is multiplied by 3
It stays the same
It increases by 3
Every deviation is multiplied by 3 and variance uses squared deviations, so it scales by 3^2 = 9. The standard deviation scales by 3.
For a normal distribution, roughly what share of values lies within one standard deviation of the mean?
About 68%
About 50%
About 95%
About 99.7%
The 68-95-99.7 rule gives about 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD.
IQ scores are modeled as normal with mean 100 and SD 15. What is the z-score of a score of 130?
z = (x - mean) / SD = (130 - 100) / 15 = 2, so the score is two standard deviations above the mean.
In hypothesis testing, what is a Type I error?
Rejecting a null hypothesis that is true
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Using the wrong test statistic
Choosing too small a sample
A Type I error is a false positive, and its probability is the significance level alpha. Failing to reject a false null is a Type II error.
What is the correct definition of a p-value?
The probability, under H0, of data at least as extreme as observed
The probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true given the data
The probability that the result happened by chance alone
A p-value is computed under the null hypothesis. It is not the probability that H0 or H1 is true.
A test with significance level alpha = 0.05 gives p = 0.03. What is the correct decision?
Reject the null hypothesis
Fail to reject the null hypothesis
Accept the null hypothesis as true
Repeat the test until p < 0.01
Since p < alpha, the result is statistically significant at the 5% level, so H0 is rejected.
A study reports p = 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?
Data this extreme would be rare if H0 were true
There is a 3% chance that H0 is true
There is a 97% chance that the observed effect is real
The effect size measured in the study is 3%
The p-value describes data under H0, not the probability of hypotheses, and it says nothing direct about effect size.
What is the correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval for a mean?
About 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean
The true mean lies in this interval with 95% probability
95% of the data values lie in this interval
The sample mean will be in this range 95% of the time
The 95% refers to the long-run success rate of the method. Once computed, a specific interval either contains the fixed true mean or not.
Other things equal, you quadruple the sample size. What happens to the width of a confidence interval for the mean?
It is roughly halved
It is roughly quartered
It stays the same
It roughly doubles
The standard error is SD / sqrt(n), so multiplying n by 4 divides the width by sqrt(4) = 2.
How does a 99% confidence interval compare with a 95% interval from the same data?
It is wider
It is narrower
It has the same width
It has a new center
Higher confidence needs a larger critical value (about 2.58 instead of 1.96), so the interval is wider around the same estimate.
A fitted linear regression is y = 3 + 2x. How do you interpret the coefficient 2?
Each unit increase in x adds 2 to predicted y
Predicted y equals 2 when x equals 0
Each unit increase in x doubles predicted y
The model explains 2% of the variance in y
The slope is the change in the predicted y per one-unit change in x. The intercept 3 is the prediction at x = 0. Regression alone does not prove causation.
A linear regression has R^2 = 0.8. What does this mean?
The model explains 80% of the variance in y
80% of predictions are exactly correct
The slope of the line is 0.8
The correlation between x and y is 0.8
R^2 is the share of variance in the target explained by the model. In simple regression it equals the squared correlation, so r is about 0.89, not 0.8.
Ordinary least squares regression chooses coefficients that minimize what?
The sum of squared residuals
The sum of absolute residuals
The largest single residual
The number of points off the line
OLS minimizes the squared vertical distances. Minimizing absolute residuals is least absolute deviations, which is more robust to outliers.
probability: You toss two fair coins. What is the probability that both land heads?
The tosses are independent, so the probability is 1/2 * 1/2 = 1/4.
A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A and B)?
For independent events P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B) = 0.5 * 0.4 = 0.2.
A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. Are they independent?
No, since P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) = 0.12
Yes, since they cannot affect each other
Yes, since P(A) + P(B) is less than 1
It cannot be decided from this data
If A happens, B cannot, so knowing A changes the probability of B. Disjoint events with positive probabilities are always dependent.
You roll a fair six-sided die twice. What is the probability of getting at least one six?
Use the complement: P(no six) = (5/6)^2 = 25/36, so P(at least one) = 1 - 25/36 = 11/36. Adding 1/6 + 1/6 = 12/36 double counts double six.
A fair die is rolled and you are told the result is even. What is the probability that it is a 6?
Conditioning shrinks the sample space to {2, 4, 6}, and 6 is one of three equally likely outcomes.
Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that both are aces?
P = 4/52 * 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221. 1/169 would be the answer with replacement.
P(A and B) = 0.1 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A | B)?
By definition P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B) = 0.1 / 0.4 = 0.25.
A disease affects 1% of people. A test detects it 99% of the time and gives a false positive 5% of the time. A random person tests positive. Roughly what is the chance they have the disease?
About 17%
About 99%
About 95%
About 50%
P(+) = 0.01*0.99 + 0.99*0.05 = 0.0594, and P(D | +) = 0.0099 / 0.0594, about 0.17. The low base rate makes most positives false.
Which formula is Bayes' theorem?
P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B)
P(A|B) = P(A) P(B) / P(B|A)
P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(B) / P(A)
P(A|B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(B|A)
It follows from writing P(A and B) as both P(A|B) P(B) and P(B|A) P(A) and solving for P(A|B).
X is a continuous random variable with a density. What is P(X = 2.5) exactly?
Exactly 0
The value f(2.5)
1 / range of X
Half of f(2.5)
For a continuous variable, probability is the area under the density, and a single point has zero width, so its probability is 0.
X is Binomial with n = 20 trials and success probability p = 0.25. What is Var(X)?
The variance of a binomial is np(1 - p) = 20 * 0.25 * 0.75 = 3.75. The mean np is 5.
A Bernoulli random variable has success probability p = 0.3. What is its variance?
X is uniform on the interval [0, 0.5]. What is the value of its probability density function inside that interval?
The density must integrate to 1 over a width of 0.5, so it equals 1 / 0.5 = 2. A density can exceed 1; only probabilities cannot.
Which condition must every probability density function f satisfy?
f(x) >= 0 and its integral over all x equals 1
f(x) <= 1 for every x and it integrates to 1
f is symmetric around its mean value
f(x) > 0 for every real number x
Densities are nonnegative and integrate to 1. They may exceed 1, be asymmetric, and be zero outside a range.
Waiting time X follows an exponential distribution with rate lambda = 2 per minute. What is E[X]?
0.5 minutes
2 minutes
4 minutes
0.25 minutes
The mean of an exponential distribution is 1 / lambda = 1 / 2. 0.25 is its variance, 1 / lambda^2.
What is the expected value of one roll of a fair six-sided die?
E = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 21 / 6 = 3.5. The expected value need not be a possible outcome.
A random variable X has E[X] = 4. What is E[2X + 3]?
Expectation is linear: E[2X + 3] = 2 E[X] + 3 = 8 + 3 = 11.
Which statement holds for any two random variables X and Y with finite means, even if they are dependent?
E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]
Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y)
E[XY] = E[X] E[Y]
P(X, Y) = P(X) P(Y)
Linearity of expectation needs no independence. The variance rule needs uncorrelated variables, and the other two need independence.
You pay 1 dollar to play. If a fair die shows 6 you receive 5 dollars, otherwise nothing. What is your expected net gain per game?
About -0.17 dollars
About +0.17 dollars
About -0.83 dollars
Exactly 0 dollars
Expected payout is 5 * 1/6, about 0.83, minus the 1 dollar cost gives about -1/6, so you lose about 17 cents per game on average.
What does the law of large numbers state?
The sample mean approaches the expected value as n grows
The sample mean becomes normally distributed
After a long losing streak a win becomes more likely
Every outcome eventually occurs equally often in any sample
LLN is about convergence of averages. The normal shape of the sample mean is the central limit theorem, and streaks do not change independent probabilities.
calculus: What is the derivative of sin(x^2) with respect to x?
By the chain rule, the outer derivative cos(x^2) is multiplied by the inner derivative 2x.
What is the derivative of e^(3x) with respect to x?
The chain rule multiplies e^(3x) by the derivative of 3x, which is 3. The power rule does not apply to exponentials.
What is the derivative of ln(x^2 + 1) with respect to x?
The derivative of ln(u) is u' / u, and here u' = 2x.
The sigmoid is s(x) = 1 / (1 + e^(-x)). What is its derivative?
Differentiating gives e^(-x) / (1 + e^(-x))^2, which simplifies to s(x)(1 - s(x)). Its maximum is 0.25 at x = 0.
What is the derivative of x e^x with respect to x?
By the product rule: 1 * e^x + x * e^x = (x + 1) e^x.
For f(x, y) = x^2 y + y^3, what is the partial derivative with respect to x?
Treat y as a constant: x^2 y becomes 2xy and y^3 becomes 0.
For f(x, y) = x^2 y + y^3, what is the partial derivative with respect to y?
Treat x as a constant: x^2 y becomes x^2 and y^3 becomes 3y^2.
What is the gradient of f(x, y) = x^2 + 3y at the point (1, 2)?
The gradient is (df/dx, df/dy) = (2x, 3), which at x = 1 is (2, 3).
At a point where the gradient of f is nonzero, in which direction does f increase fastest?
In the direction of the gradient
The directional derivative is the dot product of the gradient with a unit vector, which is largest along the gradient. Gradient descent steps the opposite way.
In which direction is the directional derivative of a differentiable f equal to zero?
The dot product of the gradient with a perpendicular unit vector is zero. That direction is tangent to the level curve.
What is the value of the integral of x^2 from 0 to 1?
An antiderivative is x^3 / 3, and evaluating from 0 to 1 gives 1/3.
What is the value of the integral of sin(x) from 0 to pi?
An antiderivative is -cos(x), so the value is -cos(pi) + cos(0) = 1 + 1 = 2.
Using integration by parts, what is the indefinite integral of x e^x?
With u = x and dv = e^x dx: x e^x minus the integral of e^x, which gives x e^x - e^x + C. Differentiate to check.
If F(x) is the integral of f(t) from 0 to x, with f continuous, what is F'(x)?
This is the fundamental theorem of calculus: differentiating an integral with a variable upper limit returns the integrand.
What is the coefficient of x^3 in the Maclaurin series of e^x?
e^x = sum of x^n / n!, so the coefficient of x^3 is 1 / 3! = 1/6.
What are the first two nonzero terms of the Maclaurin series of sin(x)?
sin(x) = x - x^3/3! + x^5/5! - ..., with only odd powers. 1 - x^2/2 begins the series for cos(x).
Using a first-order Taylor approximation of sqrt(x) around x = 4, what is the estimate for sqrt(4.1)?
f(4) = 2 and f'(x) = 1 / (2 sqrt(x)) = 0.25 at 4, so the estimate is 2 + 0.25 * 0.1 = 2.025.
What kind of critical point does f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2 have at the origin?
It is not a critical point
The gradient (2x, -2y) is zero at the origin, but f rises along the x axis and falls along the y axis.
At a critical point of a twice differentiable f(x, y), the Hessian is positive definite. What can you conclude?
The point is a local minimum
The point is a local maximum
The point is a saddle point
A positive definite Hessian means f curves upward in every direction. Negative definite means a maximum, and mixed signs mean a saddle.
Where is the critical point of f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 6y?
Setting 2x - 4 = 0 and 2y + 6 = 0 gives x = 2 and y = -3. Completing the square shows it is the minimum.
optimization: Gradient descent minimizes f(x) = x^2 from x0 = 3 with learning rate 0.1. What is x1?
The gradient at 3 is 2 * 3 = 6, so x1 = 3 - 0.1 * 6 = 2.4.
Gradient descent on f(x) = x^2 uses learning rate 1.5. What happens to the iterates?
They flip sign and grow, so the method diverges
They oscillate but shrink, so they converge to 0
They converge slowly and monotonically to 0
They stay at the starting point forever
The update is x - 1.5 * 2x = -2x, so the magnitude doubles every step. Rates below 1 converge for this function.
How does stochastic gradient descent differ from full-batch gradient descent?
It uses the gradient of one example or a small batch
It uses second derivatives of the loss instead of gradients
It picks a random step direction at each iteration
It needs a convex loss function to work at all
Each SGD step is cheap but noisy, because the mini-batch gradient only estimates the full gradient. The noise can even help escape poor regions.
What does adding momentum to gradient descent do?
Accumulates past gradients to smooth and speed up updates
Doubles the learning rate after each epoch to speed up training
Resets the weights to their start whenever the loss rises
Computes exact second derivatives of the loss
Momentum keeps a decaying average of gradients, which dampens oscillation across steep directions and builds speed along consistent ones.
The Adam optimizer keeps exponential moving averages of which quantities?
The gradients and the squared gradients
The weights and the squared weights
The losses and the learning rates
The gradients and the Hessian
The first moment acts like momentum, and the second moment scales each parameter's step, similar to RMSProp.
Why does Adam apply bias correction to its moment estimates?
The averages start at zero and are biased low early on
To stop the learning rate from ever decaying during training
To make the loss function convex near the start
To remove label noise from the gradient estimates
Starting both moving averages at 0 makes the first estimates too small. Dividing by (1 - beta^t) corrects this, which matters most in early steps.
What does AdamW change compared with Adam plus an L2 penalty in the loss?
It decouples weight decay from the adaptive gradient step
It removes the second-moment estimate entirely
It replaces standard momentum with Nesterov momentum updates
It disables bias correction for both moments
With Adam, an L2 term is rescaled by the adaptive denominator. AdamW decouples weight decay so every weight shrinks at the intended rate.
What is the key advantage of minimizing a convex function?
Any local minimum is also a global minimum
Gradient descent needs no learning rate
The minimum is always at zero
The minimum is always unique
Convexity rules out spurious local minima. The minimizer need not be unique (a flat bottom), unless the function is strictly convex.
Which of these functions of one real variable is convex on the whole real line?
f(x) = e^x
f(x) = sin(x)
e^x has second derivative e^x > 0 everywhere. x^3 is concave for x < 0, -x^2 is concave, and sin(x) alternates.
A twice differentiable function f of one variable is convex exactly when which condition holds?
f''(x) >= 0 for all x
f'(x) >= 0 for all x
f(x) >= 0 for all x
f''(x) = 0 at some x
A nonnegative second derivative means the slope never decreases. f'(x) >= 0 only means f is nondecreasing.
f and g are convex functions. Which of these is guaranteed to be convex?
max(f(x), g(x))
min(f(x), g(x))
f(x) - g(x)
f(x) * g(x)
The pointwise maximum of convex functions is convex. The minimum, difference and product can fail, for example x^2 - 2x^2 = -x^2.
At a constrained optimum of f subject to g(x) = c found with Lagrange multipliers, what relationship holds (with regular constraints)?
grad f = lambda * grad g
grad f = lambda * g
grad f = 0 and g(x) = c
f(x) = lambda * g(x)
At the optimum, the level set of f is tangent to the constraint, so their gradients are parallel. grad f = 0 is the unconstrained condition.
What is the maximum of f(x, y) = xy subject to x + y = 10?
Lagrange conditions give y = lambda and x = lambda, so x = y = 5 and xy = 25.
What is the minimum of x^2 + y^2 subject to x + y = 2?
Lagrange conditions give 2x = 2y, so x = y = 1 and the value is 1 + 1 = 2.
How is a Lagrange multiplier lambda interpreted in a constrained optimization problem?
The sensitivity of the optimal value to the constraint level
The step size used by the optimizer at each iteration
The number of constraints that are active at the optimal point
The curvature of the objective function at the optimum
lambda measures how sensitive the optimum is to relaxing the constraint, which is why economists call it a shadow price.
At a point, the gradient of a loss is zero and the Hessian has both positive and negative eigenvalues. What is this point?
A saddle point
A global minimum
A local minimum
A local maximum
The loss curves up in some directions and down in others. In high-dimensional neural network losses, saddle points are very common.
Gradient descent runs on f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2, which has minima at x = 1 and x = -1. It starts at exactly x0 = 0. What happens?
It stays at x = 0, where the gradient is zero
It moves to the minimum at x = 1
It moves to the minimum at x = -1
It oscillates between x = 1 and x = -1 forever
f'(x) = 4x^3 - 4x is 0 at x = 0, a local maximum, so the update does nothing. This is one reason weights are initialized randomly.
Which loss is standard for multi-class classification with softmax outputs?
Cross-entropy
Mean squared error
Hinge loss on raw labels
Mean absolute error
Cross-entropy is the negative log likelihood of the true class, and with softmax it gives well-behaved gradients. MSE is mainly for regression.
You must predict a single constant c for a set of targets. Which c minimizes the mean squared error?
The mean of the targets
The median of the targets
The mode of the targets
The midrange of the targets
Setting the derivative of the sum of (y - c)^2 to zero gives c = mean. Minimizing mean absolute error gives the median instead.
What effect does adding an L2 penalty lambda * ||w||^2 to the training loss have?
It pushes weights toward smaller values
It sets many weights to exactly zero
It raises the learning rate
It makes the loss non-convex
L2 shrinks weights smoothly and reduces overfitting. Exact zeros are typical of the L1 penalty.
